body:
The meaning of reproductive health

Reproductive health means well-being in matters relating to reproduction, including physical, emotional and social aspects. It is not limited to the normal functioning of reproductive organs.

Reproductive health includes accurate information about puberty and sexuality, prevention of sexually transmitted infections, appropriate care during pregnancy and childbirth, safe and voluntary family planning, and access to care for reproductive-health problems.

Why family planning matters

Family planning enables individuals and couples to make informed, voluntary decisions about whether and when to have children and how to space pregnancies. Access to reliable contraceptive information and services can reduce unintended pregnancies and related health risks.

Contraception refers to methods used to prevent pregnancy. Methods differ in their action, effectiveness, reversibility and ability to protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Major contraceptive methods

MethodBasic principleImportant distinction
Barrier methodsPhysically prevent sperm from reaching the eggCondoms also reduce transmission of HIV and other STIs.
Hormonal methodsUse hormones to suppress ovulation, alter cervical mucus or produce other contraceptive effectsInclude various pills, injections and implants; they do not protect against STIs.
Intrauterine devicesA device placed in the uterus prevents pregnancyCopper-bearing and hormonal types are long-acting and reversible.
Fertility-awareness methodsIdentify potentially fertile days to avoid unprotected intercourseEffectiveness depends on correct use; cycle variation can make prediction difficult.
Permanent methodsPrevent sperm or egg transport through a surgical procedureVasectomy and female sterilisation are intended to be permanent.

Condoms are distinctive because they can reduce the risk of both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. Their effectiveness depends on consistent and correct use.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) include copper-bearing devices and hormone-releasing devices. Both are highly effective reversible contraceptives, but neither protects against STIs.

Vasectomy prevents sperm from entering semen by blocking or interrupting the vas deferens. Female sterilisation prevents egg and sperm from meeting by blocking or interrupting the fallopian tubes. These methods are intended for people who do not want future pregnancies.

Temporary contraception and emergency contraception

Temporary methods allow contraception to be discontinued when pregnancy is desired. Reversibility does not mean every method works in the same way or has the same duration.

Emergency contraception is used after unprotected intercourse or a contraceptive failure to prevent pregnancy. Emergency contraceptive pills mainly work by preventing or delaying ovulation. A copper-bearing IUD can also be used for emergency contraception when clinically appropriate.

Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy; it does not terminate an established pregnancy. It must not be confused with medical termination of pregnancy.

Breastfeeding and natural spacing of pregnancies

Exclusive or nearly exclusive breastfeeding can temporarily suppress ovulation after childbirth. The lactational amenorrhoea method relies on 3 conditions: the infant is younger than 6 months, menstruation has not returned and breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive. Its protection declines when these conditions are no longer met.

This temporary contraceptive effect is different from the nutritional and health benefits of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding alone should not be assumed to prevent pregnancy indefinitely.

India's public-sector family-planning choices

India's public health system includes several named contraceptive options. Examples include Nirodh condoms, Mala-N combined oral contraceptive pills, Chhaya non-hormonal oral contraceptive pills, the Antara injectable contraceptive programme and copper intrauterine devices.

The availability of multiple methods supports informed choice. The appropriate method depends on individual circumstances, preferences and medical eligibility. Family planning is based on voluntary participation, not compulsory use of a particular method.

Reproductive healthcare as a continuum

Good reproductive healthcare extends across adolescence, the period before pregnancy, pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period. Education and preventive services are especially valuable before a health problem develops.

Prelims focus

  • Reproductive health includes physical, emotional and social well-being.
  • Condoms reduce the risk of pregnancy and transmission of many STIs.
  • Copper-bearing and hormonal IUDs are long-acting reversible methods.
  • Vasectomy and female sterilisation are intended as permanent contraception.
  • Chhaya is a non-hormonal oral contraceptive option in India's public programme.
  • Trap: Emergency contraception is not the same as abortion.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 4, Reproductive Health, sections 4.1–4.5; WHO, Family Planning/Contraception Methods, fact sheet dated 3 July 2025; WHO, Intrauterine Devices, fact sheet dated 22 January 2026; WHO, Emergency Contraception, fact sheet dated 9 November 2021; National Health Mission, Family Planning, public-sector contraceptive methods; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A continuous pathway links adolescence, planning, pregnancy, childbirth and postnatal life with their distinct reproductive-health needs.
pictures.caption: Reproductive-health needs change across different stages of life.

title: Reproductive Health, Family Planning and Contraceptive Methods

body:
What are sexually transmitted infections?

Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections that can spread through sexual contact. They may be caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites. Some can also spread through infected blood or from a mother to her child.

An STI may cause symptoms, but it may also remain unnoticed. Therefore, the absence of symptoms does not prove that a person has no STI.

Important sexually transmitted infections

InfectionType of pathogenKey fact
GonorrhoeaBacteriumMay affect reproductive organs and cause complications if untreated
SyphilisBacteriumCan affect multiple body systems and be transmitted during pregnancy
Chlamydial infectionBacteriumMay be asymptomatic and can damage reproductive health
TrichomoniasisProtozoan parasiteA curable parasitic STI
Genital herpesHerpes simplex virusCan produce recurrent symptoms
Hepatitis BHepatitis B virusCan affect the liver; vaccination provides protection
HPV infectionHuman papillomavirusPersistent high-risk types can cause cervical and other cancers
HIV infectionHuman immunodeficiency virusWeakens the immune system and can progress to AIDS

HIV infection and AIDS are not the same

HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus. It attacks important cells of the immune system, especially CD4 T lymphocytes.

AIDS, or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, associated with severe immune damage and characteristic illnesses.

A person can live with HIV without having AIDS. With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV infection can be managed as a chronic condition, and progression to AIDS can be prevented in many people.

How HIV spreads

HIV can be transmitted through infected blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids and breast milk. Important routes include sexual exposure, sharing contaminated injecting equipment, unsafe blood exposure, and transmission during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.

HIV is not transmitted through ordinary social contact such as shaking hands, hugging, sharing meals or using the same drinking-water source. It is also not transmitted by mosquito bites.

Why STI prevention matters

Untreated STIs may cause complications such as infertility, pregnancy complications and increased vulnerability to other infections. Certain infections, including persistent high-risk HPV infection, can increase cancer risk.

Important prevention measures include:

  • Consistent and correct condom use, which reduces transmission risk but does not completely eliminate every STI risk.
  • Vaccination against hepatitis B and HPV where appropriate.
  • Safe blood supplies and sterile needles.
  • Access to confidential testing and timely healthcare.
  • Appropriate antenatal screening and prevention of mother-to-child transmission.

Condoms offer important protection against infections transmitted through sexual fluids. However, they may not completely prevent infections that can spread through contact with affected skin outside the covered area.

HPV and cervical-cancer prevention

Persistent infection with certain high-risk types of human papillomavirus can cause changes in cervical cells that may eventually develop into cervical cancer.

HPV vaccination helps prevent infection with important cancer-causing types. Appropriate cervical screening can identify precancerous changes or cancer at an earlier stage. Vaccination and screening serve different but complementary preventive purposes.

Prelims focus

  • Gonorrhoea and syphilis are bacterial STIs.
  • Trichomoniasis is caused by a protozoan parasite.
  • HIV is the causative virus; AIDS is an advanced stage of HIV infection.
  • HIV does not spread through hugging, shared food or mosquito bites.
  • HPV and hepatitis B are infections for which preventive vaccines are available.
  • Trap: A person may have an STI without noticeable symptoms.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 4, Reproductive Health, section 4.4, Sexually Transmitted Diseases; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.3, AIDS; WHO, Sexually Transmitted Infections, fact sheet dated 10 September 2025; WHO, HIV and AIDS, fact sheet dated 27 July 2026; WHO, Cervical Cancer, fact sheet dated 3 July 2026; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: HIV can spread through specific blood, sexual, injecting and parent-to-child exposures, but not handshakes, hugs, shared food or water, or mosquito bites.
pictures.caption: HIV transmission requires specific exposure routes, not ordinary social contact.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections, HIV and Reproductive-Health Protection

body:
Clinical care and public health have different primary purposes

Clinical medicine focuses on identifying and managing health problems in individual patients. Public health focuses on protecting and improving the health of populations.

The 2 approaches support each other. A clinician may diagnose tuberculosis in a patient. Public-health services may use that information to monitor disease patterns, support contact assessment and organise prevention activities.

Public health does not replace clinical diagnosis or treatment. Its distinctive concern is the health of groups, communities and populations.

Prevention has different levels

LevelMain objectiveExample
Primary preventionPrevent disease before it occursVaccination, safe water, tobacco prevention
Secondary preventionIdentify disease early and enable timely interventionScreening for hypertension or cervical precancer
Tertiary preventionReduce complications, disability or further harm from established diseaseRehabilitation after a stroke

For example, avoiding tobacco is primary prevention of tobacco-related disease. Measuring blood pressure in an apparently healthy adult can support secondary prevention by identifying possible hypertension. Rehabilitation after a disabling stroke is an example of tertiary prevention.

Screening is not confirmation of disease

Screening is the use of a test or assessment to identify people who may have a disease or an increased likelihood of disease, often before symptoms appear.

Diagnosis is the process of determining whether a person actually has a particular condition, using clinical assessment and appropriate investigations.

A screening test may produce a false positive, suggesting disease where it is absent, or a false negative, failing to identify disease that is present. Consequently, a positive screening result commonly requires further evaluation, and a negative result does not always exclude disease.

Incidence and prevalence

These 2 terms describe different aspects of disease occurrence in a population.

  • Incidence: The occurrence of new cases in a defined population during a specified period. It helps describe the risk or rate of developing disease.
  • Prevalence: The total number or proportion of people who have a disease at a specified time or during a specified period, including both existing and newly developed cases.

If 100 people already have a chronic condition at the start of a year and 20 additional people develop it during that year, the 20 represent new incident cases. The number of people living with the condition at the end of the year depends on those new cases as well as recovery, deaths and other changes.

Prevalence is often high for diseases that last a long time, even when relatively few new cases occur. Incidence and prevalence therefore cannot be treated as synonyms.

Endemic, outbreak, epidemic and pandemic

Endemic refers to the usual or continuing presence of a disease within a particular geographical area or population. The level may vary over time.

An outbreak is a localised occurrence of cases above what is normally expected. An epidemic is the occurrence of disease cases above the expected level in a defined population or area. A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents and affects large numbers of people.

These terms describe patterns of disease spread. They do not identify the pathogen or specify a particular treatment.

Public-health surveillance

Disease surveillance is the systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and use of health information to guide public-health action.

For example, an increase in reported dengue cases in a district may prompt an investigation, mosquito-source reduction, public communication and closer monitoring. A reported increase is a reason to investigate; the reports alone do not prove the exact source of infection.

Elimination and eradication

Elimination of a disease generally refers to reducing its incidence to zero in a defined geographical area, with continued measures needed to prevent its return. Eradication means permanent worldwide reduction to zero incidence of infection caused by a particular agent, after which further interventions against that agent are no longer required.

A national goal to eliminate a disease is not proof that elimination has already been achieved.

Prelims focus

  • Primary prevention acts before disease develops.
  • Screening is commonly part of secondary prevention.
  • Tertiary prevention reduces disability or complications from established disease.
  • Incidence concerns new cases; prevalence includes existing cases.
  • Surveillance provides information for population-level public-health action.
  • Trap: A positive screening result is not automatically a confirmed clinical diagnosis.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, sections 13.1–13.3; WHO, Noncommunicable Diseases, fact sheet dated 25 September 2025, sections on detection and screening; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Programme for Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases, Operational Guidelines, sections on population-based screening and referral; sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: As disease progresses, primary prevention avoids disease, secondary prevention detects it early, and tertiary prevention limits complications.
pictures.caption: Prevention changes its objective as disease develops and progresses.

title: Public Health, Screening and the Measurement of Disease
